title: US Job Openings Just Hit a Two-Year High. If You Are on an H-1B or Looking for Work in America, Here Is What It Means.
excerpt: Employers posted 7.6 million openings in April, the most since March 2024. For the first time since June, there is more than one job available for every unemployed American.
body:
The American job market just did something it has not done in two years. Employers posted 7.6 million job openings in April, the highest since March 2024, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Job Openings and Labour Turnover Survey released on Tuesday. That blew past the 6.9 million economists had expected and jumped sharply from March's 6.9 million.

For the first time since June, there were more jobs available than people looking for them — 1.03 openings for every unemployed worker. The ratio had been below 1 for months, signalling a labour market that was slowly tilting away from workers. That tilt just reversed.

## What the Numbers Actually Say

The JOLTS report is not a count of hiring. It measures unfilled positions — the demand side of the labour equation. And on that front, demand surged.

But the details are more nuanced. Employers hired 5.1 million workers in April, down from 5.5 million in March. And 3 million workers quit their jobs, down from 3.2 million, suggesting people felt less confident about jumping to new roles. Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, called it "a low-hire, low-fire job market" where "workers are job clinging and not eager to leave."

The paradox is familiar to anyone who has navigated America's job market in recent years: companies are posting openings but taking longer to fill them. Hiring processes have slowed, requirements have tightened, and the gap between a posting and an actual offer letter has widened.

Elizabeth Renter, senior economist at NerdWallet, urged caution. "Job seekers now can be hopeful that the April bump in job openings will translate to more hiring, but because today's data is subject to revision and because a job listing doesn't always end in a job offer, they should stay sharp and prepare for a continued search."

## Why It Matters for NRI Workers

For the roughly 600,000 H-1B visa holders working in the United States, the JOLTS data carries specific implications.

A tighter labour market — one where employers are competing for workers — is generally better for visa holders. Companies are less likely to revoke offers, more willing to sponsor transfers, and more open to paying the premium wages that H-1B regulations require. The opposite dynamic, a soft market with more candidates than jobs, creates exactly the conditions that make sponsorship harder and layoffs more likely.

The return above 1.0 in the jobs-per-unemployed ratio is particularly significant for Indian professionals in technology, healthcare, and finance, who make up the largest share of H-1B holders. When companies need workers badly enough to keep 7.6 million positions unfilled, the leverage shifts.

For F-1 students on OPT, the data is equally relevant. A rising tide of openings means more entry-level positions and more employers willing to navigate the paperwork of hiring international graduates. For those whose OPT clocks are ticking, timing matters enormously.

## The Fed Angle

The Federal Reserve watches JOLTS data closely. Strong job openings mean the economy is healthy, which in turn means the Fed has less pressure to cut interest rates to stimulate growth. In fact, the data gives the central bank more room to keep rates elevated to fight inflation, which has been rising because of the Iran war's energy crunch. Oil is trading near $91 per barrel, up more than 30 per cent since the conflict began.

Fed officials are widely expected to hold rates steady at their next meeting later this month. Friday's non-farm payrolls report for May will provide a more current snapshot, but the JOLTS data sets the tone.

For NRI investors with exposure to US equities, higher-for-longer rates mean continued pressure on growth stocks and real estate, but potential benefits for fixed-income investments and savings accounts. The 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 4.43 per cent on Tuesday, a three-week low, suggesting bond markets are cautiously optimistic that the economy can absorb higher oil prices without tipping into recession.

## The Bigger Picture

The US labour market has been remarkably resilient through a cascade of shocks — tariffs, immigration restrictions, and a war that has sent energy prices surging. The April JOLTS data suggests that resilience is holding.

For the Indian diaspora, the implications ripple across generations. Parents on H-1B visas benefit from employer demand. Students benefit from more OPT opportunities. Investors benefit from an economy that is generating enough activity to keep 7.6 million positions open.

But JOLTS data is famously subject to revision, and a single month does not make a trend. The real test comes Friday, when the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes hiring and unemployment data for May. That report will reveal whether the surge in openings is translating into actual paycheques — or whether America's employers are posting help-wanted signs without following through.
author: Diaspora Desk
